arguments.title: Tenant was delinquent in rent and the lock change was expressly authorized by the lease and Section 93.002(c)(3)
arguments.summary: Tenant admits it paid nothing on August 1 and unilaterally 'applied' a disputed repair cost against rent. Section 4.4 forbids withholding or offset for any alleged Landlord default and Section 7.4 repeats that self-help costs may not be offset against Rent. A tenant delinquent in at least part of the rent may have its locks changed under Section 93.002(c)(3), and Section 15.2(c) of the lease adopts that remedy. Landlord posted a notice with a name and telephone number as both the lease and subsection (f) require.

refs.quote: Tenant shall not withhold, abate, or offset Rent on account of any alleged default by Landlord
changing the door locks of a tenant who is delinquent in paying at least part of the rent

assumptions: The posted notice stated the name and telephone number as described in Tenant's own email.
evidentiary_weaknesses: The $1,500 fee demand complicates the key-release condition in subsection (f).
anticipated_counterarguments: Tenant will argue the fee rendered the exclusion unlawful and that an Event of Default had not matured.
arguments.confidence_rationale: Non-payment is admitted in writing and the no-offset clauses are explicit.

arguments.title: The rooftop unit is Tenant's responsibility under the specific language of Section 7.2
arguments.summary: Section 7.2 assigns to Tenant 'all heating, ventilation, and air-conditioning equipment exclusively serving the Premises' and requires a quarterly maintenance contract. The vendor identified the failed unit as the rooftop unit 'serving Suite 140'. Section 1.10 covers systems serving the Building 'generally'; a dedicated unit does not. A specific allocation controls over a general definition, and Tenant has never produced the maintenance contract the lease required, which bears on causation of an end-of-life compressor failure.

refs.quote: all heating, ventilation, and air-conditioning equipment exclusively serving the Premises

assumptions: The unit serves only Suite 140 (consistent with the vendor's description).
evidentiary_weaknesses: Section 1.10 expressly mentions 'rooftop equipment', and Section 2.2's commencement warranty suggests Landlord treated the unit as within its sphere at delivery.
anticipated_counterarguments: Tenant will read 'including rooftop equipment' as decisive and invoke the Section 2.2 representation.
arguments.confidence_rationale: The specific wording favors Landlord, but the definition's reference to rooftop equipment leaves real ambiguity.

arguments.title: Even if Landlord owed the repair, Tenant forfeited reimbursement by skipping the Section 7.4 procedure and offsetting rent
arguments.summary: Section 7.4 allows self-help only after Landlord fails to act within the Section 7.1 period and after an additional ten days' written notice of intent to repair, followed by an invoice payable in 30 days. Tenant announced on June 21 that it was proceeding immediately, never sent an invoice with supporting documentation, and instead deducted the amount from rent, which Section 7.4 and Section 4.4 prohibit. Tenant's email also was not 'notice' under Section 17.2.

refs.quote: after an additional ten (10) days' written notice to Landlord specifying Tenant's intent to perform the repair
Since Landlord has not responded to our June 21 email or reimbursed us, we are applying the $8,400 against August rent

assumptions: No separate invoice or formal notice was sent beyond the emails in the file.
evidentiary_weaknesses: Landlord's own agents corresponded by email throughout, which Tenant may argue waived strict notice formalities or acknowledged receipt.
anticipated_counterarguments: Tenant may argue an emergency excused the waiting period and that Landlord's refusal made further notice futile.
arguments.confidence_rationale: The procedural steps in Section 7.4 are explicit and the email record shows they were not followed.

arguments.title: Notice of default was properly given and the cure period expired before the lock change
arguments.summary: The August 11 letter is captioned as sent by certified mail, return receipt requested, and Landlord's principal confirmed mailing on August 11. Under Section 17.1(c) notice is deemed given three business days after certified mailing regardless of receipt, so notice was given no later than August 14 and the ten-day cure ran out by August 24, before the August 26 lock change. Tenant's August 26 email acknowledging 'the August 11 email attachment' also supplies the written acknowledgment contemplated by Section 17.2.

refs.quote: VIA CERTIFIED MAIL, RETURN RECEIPT REQUESTED, AND ELECTRONIC MAIL
three (3) business days after deposit in the United States mail, certified, return receipt requested

assumptions: Landlord can produce the certified mail receipt.
evidentiary_weaknesses: No mailing receipt is in the file; Tenant denies receipt.
Landlord's own letter counted ten days from the letter date rather than from deemed delivery.
anticipated_counterarguments: Tenant will argue the burden to prove mailing is Landlord's and that absent proof the cure period never began.
arguments.confidence_rationale: Deemed-delivery language is favorable but proof of mailing is missing from the record.

overall_assessment: Landlord's core position is simple: rent was unpaid, offset was contractually prohibited, and the lease plus Section 93.002 authorized a lock change. Landlord's exposure lies in the $1,500 fee and the condition placed on releasing the key, and in proving that notice was mailed.
